1380.title: The Saint Michael prayer (1886)
1380.hook: Leo XIII's prayer for protection, once said after every Mass
1380.howItsDone: Some Catholics pray the Saint Michael prayer daily, and some parishes say it together at the end of Mass; it asks the archangel's protection against evil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, medals and scapulars: reminders you can touch, never a password. Your line was not a charm.

There was a time when a quiet Mass ended differently. The priest finished, and nobody left. He knelt at the foot of the altar, the people knelt with him, and together they prayed a few more prayers aloud. One wasn't addressed to God the Father, or to Mary, but to an angel, and it began by asking him to defend us in battle. Some parishes have started saying it again after Mass.
screen: `NOBODY LEFT.` → `A FEW MORE PRAYERS, KNEELING.` → `ONE OF THEM: TO AN ANGEL.`

segments.voice: The Apocalypse says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And there was a great battle in heaven, Michael and his angels fought with the dragon." In the book of Daniel, Michael is a great prince who stands up for his people. Scripture gives him the role of protector. Pope Leo the Thirteenth wrote a short prayer to Michael in Latin and added it to the prayers said kneeling at the end of Low Mass. A story people tell says he wrote it after a frightening vision during Mass. There's no firm record of that, and the prayer doesn't need it. When the liturgy was reformed after the Second Vatican Council, those prayers at the end of Mass were dropped. The Saint Michael prayer itself stayed in Catholic life. Pope John Paul the Second later urged Catholics to pray it, and some parishes have brought it back. Then what it asks. It asks Michael to defend us in battle and to be a protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil. It asks God, humbly, to rebuke him. And it asks Michael, by the power of God, to drive Satan and the evil spirits who roam the world back into hell. Strong words. But notice the order: even the warrior angel acts by God's power, not his own. Which battle? Paul writes to the Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims: "For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood." Not against the coworker, the ex, the neighbor with the barking dog, the people on the other side of an argument. Whatever this prayer is fighting, it's never a person.
screen: `MICHAEL FOUGHT THE DRAGON.` · `LEO THE THIRTEENTH, AFTER LOW MASS.` · `BY THE POWER OF GOD.` · `NOT AGAINST FLESH AND BLOOD.` · then, large: `DEFEND US IN BATTLE.`

segments.voice: If you know the Saint Michael prayer, or have it on a card, and you pray, say it once, slowly; if not, stay with its opening words, defend us in battle. Bring to mind one struggle you're in right now, then do the hard part: separate the struggle from the people in it, and let anyone you've been treating as the enemy step out of the frame. What's left is the real fight; breathe there.
The Saint Michael prayer. Pope Leo the Thirteenth's short prayer asking the archangel to defend us in battle, once said at the end of Low Mass, still prayed by some Catholics today.
Your line: defend us in battle. Even the warrior angel acts by God's power, not his own. See you tomorrow.

1381.title: Holy water at home
1381.hook: a font by the door, used when leaving and returning
1381.howItsDone: Catholics bless themselves with holy water at the church door, and some families keep a small font of blessed water by the front door at home, making the sign of the cross when leaving and returning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Saint Michael prayer: protection by God's power, never against flesh and blood. Your line was defend us in battle.

A small cup screwed to the wall beside a front door, between the light switch and the hook for keys. Sometimes it's a ceramic shell with a saint painted on it. Sometimes it's bone dry; nobody remembered to refill it. A child heading out to school dips two fingers, touches forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other, and is out the door before the shape is finished.
screen: `A CUP BY THE FRONT DOOR.` → `TWO FINGERS, A QUICK CROSS.` → `OUT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: A Catholic walking into a church dips a hand in holy water at the door and makes the sign of the cross. The Church says it recalls baptism, the water a Christian first passed through. Now carry the font home. Families can ask a priest to bless water, take it home in a bottle, and fill a small font by the front door. The church-door gesture now happens at the house door: going out to work, coming back from the hospital, leaving for a first date. Why the door? Thresholds are where a day changes direction. You walk out into hours you can't control and come back carrying whatever they gave you. A psalm has a verse for this, in the Douay-Rheims: "May the Lord keep thy coming in and thy going out; from henceforth now and for ever." The font turns that verse into a gesture. Before the main Sunday Mass in the older Latin rite, the priest could walk through the church sprinkling the people while the choir sang Asperges me. The words come from a psalm of repentance, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed: thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow." Water at the front door says the same thing on a Tuesday morning: wash me, start me again. Like a medal, the water isn't a force field; it doesn't keep accidents off the driveway. It's a sacramental: a sign, blessed by the Church's prayer, that turns a person toward God at the moment it's easiest to forget, hand on the doorknob, keys in hand, already late.

segments.voice: If you have holy water, set it where your hand will find it at the next door you leave by; if not, a sign of the cross at the threshold will do, or a pause with your hand on the handle. If you pray, borrow the psalm's words, may the Lord keep thy coming in and thy going out; if you don't, let the doorway be one breath before the day takes you.
Holy water at home. Blessed water in a small font by the door, used for the sign of the cross going out and coming back: baptism remembered at the threshold.

1382.title: Blessings
1382.hook: homes, cars, throats, animals, fields: almost anything can be blessed
1382.howItsDone: Catholics ask priests and deacons to bless homes, cars, religious objects, animals, fields and people, often after Mass or by appointment; some parishes hold group blessings, such as the blessing of throats on Saint Blaise's feast. Parents and lay people lead some blessings themselves, such as grace at meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a small font of holy water by the front door, touched on the way out and on the way back in. Your line was going out blessed.

A church parking lot on a weekend morning. A priest in a white stole walks down a row of cars with a bucket and a sprinkler, while the drivers stand by their open doors. Weeks later he's on the church steps facing a line of dogs, a cat in a carrier, a goldfish in a jar and one very patient rabbit. Another day, after Mass, he holds two crossed candles at each throat. A farmer asks him out to a field; a young couple, to a new apartment that still smells of paint. Is there anything the Church won't bless?
screen: `A ROW OF CARS AND A SPRINKLER.` → `A LINE OF DOGS AND ONE RABBIT.` → `IS THERE ANYTHING IT WON'T BLESS?`

segments.voice: Start with Paul's first letter to Timothy, in the Douay-Rheims: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer." That's the whole theology of a car blessing in two sentences. Next, what a blessing does. The Catechism puts blessings among the sacramentals, and says every blessing praises God and prays for his gifts. Praise comes first. A blessing doesn't first change the thing; it thanks God for it and asks that it be used well. A priest blessing your car isn't installing a protective upgrade. He's praising God for the gift of getting places, and praying for the people who ride in it. Then, who blesses. Not only priests. The Catechism says lay people can preside at certain blessings, and the more a blessing touches the Church's sacramental life, the more it belongs to the ordained. So a mother can bless her children at bedtime and a family its table, while some blessings are kept for a priest or deacon. Last, the long list. The Church's book of blessings has prayers for homes, fields and harvests, animals, tools, the sick and travelers. On the feast of Saint Blaise, some parishes bless throats with two crossed candles; a story people tell says Blaise once saved a boy choking on a fishbone. The list is long because, for Catholics, ordinary life is not outside God's reach.

1383.title: Pilgrimage
1383.hook: traveling to a holy place as prayer
1383.howItsDone: Catholics make pilgrimages to shrines near and far, often in parish groups, with Mass, confession and prayer along the way; some walk the whole route on foot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessings: cars, dogs, throats, fields, a new apartment that still smelled of paint. Your line was everything can be blessed.

Two friends are walking out of Jerusalem on a Sunday, heading for a village called Emmaus. Their feet hurt, and their hearts hurt worse. The man they had hoped in has been crucified, and now there are strange reports of an empty tomb. A stranger falls into step and asks what they're talking about. They stop, faces sad, and tell him everything. Then, as they walk, he opens the scriptures to them, step after step. They don't know who he is. They only know they don't want the road to end.
screen: `TWO FRIENDS LEAVING JERUSALEM.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.` → `THEY DON'T WANT THE ROAD TO END.`

segments.voice: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place, made as prayer. Not tourism with a church stop: the trip itself is the point. The habit runs through scripture. Luke's Gospel says Jesus's parents went up to Jerusalem every year for the Passover, and took him along when he was twelve. Tradition hears some of the Psalms as songs for pilgrims going up to the Temple. One opens, in the Douay-Rheims, "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord." The Catechism says pilgrimages evoke our earthly journey toward heaven, and are traditionally special times for renewal in prayer. So the road is a picture. Every pilgrim acts out, with their legs, what the Catechism says about the whole of life: we're on the way, not yet home. Back at Emmaus, the friends press the stranger to stay, since evening is coming. At table he takes bread, blesses it and breaks it, and their eyes are opened. He vanishes. And they say to each other, "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way?" In the way: on the road, before they knew. Last, the Church calls herself a pilgrim. The Second Vatican Council speaks of the pilgrim Church on earth. A pilgrimage to a shrine is a small version of that bigger walk, done on purpose, with tired feet.

Decide that the walk itself will be the prayer, no headphones, no hurry, and a minute's sit when you arrive. If you pray, say a Hail Mary at each corner; if you don't, just notice every step.
Pilgrimage. A journey to a holy place, made as prayer, in which the road itself becomes part of the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: the road is the prayer. The arrival counts, and so does every step before it. See you tomorrow.

1384.title: The Camino de Santiago
1384.hook: walkers from everywhere follow yellow arrows to Compostela
1384.howItsDone: Pilgrims walk, cycle or ride sections of the Camino to the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, carrying a credential stamped along the way, attending pilgrim Masses and greeting one another with "buen camino."

segments.voice: Yesterday, pilgrimage, and two friends on the road to Emmaus whose hearts burned before they knew why. Your line was the road is the prayer.

A yellow arrow, painted on the corner of a stone wall in a Spanish village. Another on a lamppost. Another on a rock beside a dirt track through wheat fields. Follow them long enough and they lead to a cathedral. A woman with a scallop shell tied to her backpack passes a farmer leaning on a gate. He nods and says two words. Buen camino. Good road. Further on, a teenager with blistered feet hears it from a café owner, then from a limping pilgrim twice his age. Said that often, the words start to feel like a blessing.
screen: `YELLOW ARROWS ON STONE WALLS.` → `A SCALLOP SHELL ON A BACKPACK.` → `TWO WORDS: BUEN CAMINO.`

segments.voice: The Camino de Santiago is the Way of Saint James: a web of pilgrim routes across Spain, Portugal and France, all ending at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, in Spain's northwest corner. You met James on his feast day, back in year three. Santiago is Spanish for Saint James, the apostle, son of Zebedee and brother of John. Acts records his death in a single line, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword." That's Herod. Scripture says no more. Tradition says much more: that James had preached in Spain, that his body was carried there, and that his tomb lies beneath the cathedral. The Church honors the tradition; historians debate it. Both can be said honestly. Next, the signs. The scallop shell became the pilgrim's badge. Walkers carry a credential, a little folded booklet stamped at churches, hostels and cafés along the way. Arriving with it, a pilgrim can ask the cathedral office for a certificate called the Compostela. Then, the people. Some walk out of devotion, some out of grief, some to keep a vow, some after a hard year, some out of curiosity. The arrows don't ask why. Last, the greeting. Buen camino isn't a prayer. It's a wish shared between strangers going the same way. But it carries what Emmaus showed yesterday: the stranger who falls into step beside you may be going the same way home.

1385.title: The seven churches of Rome
1385.hook: Philip Neri's walking pilgrimage with picnics and songs
1385.howItsDone: Pilgrims in Rome walk the route of the seven churches in a single day, praying in each; some parishes and groups keep Philip Neri's custom of making it together, with music and a shared meal on the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Camino de Santiago: yellow arrows, scallop shells, and strangers wishing each other a good road. Your line was buen camino.

Early morning in Rome, centuries ago. A crowd gathers around a priest known for jokes as much as for prayer: shopkeepers, students, a few nobles, some boys from the streets. They set off on foot together, singing. They stop at one great church, pray, and walk on to the next. Midday, they sit down in a garden and eat lunch together: bread, wine, cheese, fruit. Then musicians play, and the crowd walks on, church after church, until evening. The priest is Philip Neri, and this day has a name.
screen: `A CROWD SETS OFF, SINGING.` → `PRAYER, THEN THE NEXT CHURCH.` → `LUNCH IN A GARDEN.`

segments.voice: The visit to the seven churches is an old Roman pilgrimage: one long day's walk to seven of the city's great churches. Saint Peter's. Saint Paul Outside the Walls. Saint John Lateran. Saint Mary Major. Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls. Holy Cross in Jerusalem. Saint Sebastian, by the catacombs. Pilgrims made this round before Philip; tradition says he turned it into something crowds could join. You met Philip in year three. He's remembered as the saint of joy, and stories about him are full of jokes, odd hats and teasing, which, the stories say, kept him and others from taking themselves too seriously. Why a walk? Tradition says Philip led these walks partly as a cheerful alternative to the rowdiness of carnival season. Instead of telling people what not to do, he gave them a better day out. And why the picnic? This is the surprise. A pilgrimage could have been grim and silent. Philip made eating together part of it, so sitting on the grass with strangers became part of the prayer, not a break from it. The Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity." Good, and pleasant. Both words. Last, the walk is still made. Parishes and groups in Rome keep the custom, and pilgrims trace the route on foot. The churches are far apart, the feet get tired, and the lunch still tastes good.

Picture a minute in the first, then the stretch between, a bench or a café where you'd eat, and who might come along; Philip walked in a crowd. If you pray, say one Our Father in each; if you don't, sit a minute in each and notice what's different.
The seven churches of Rome. A one-day walking pilgrimage to seven great churches, which Philip Neri made joyful with songs and a shared lunch. Today's word.

1386.title: The Holy Land
1386.hook: walking where Jesus walked, and praying for its people
1386.howItsDone: Catholics make pilgrimages to the Holy Land, often in parish groups led by a priest, celebrating Mass at shrines such as Bethlehem, Nazareth and the Holy Sepulchre; the Church also asks Catholics to pray and give for the Christians who live there and for peace in the region.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven churches of Rome, and Philip Neri's crowd singing between them, with lunch in a garden. Your line was pilgrims with a picnic.

A pilgrim kneels in a low cave under a church in Bethlehem and touches a silver star set into the floor. Days later she stands on the shore of the Sea of Galilee at dawn: fishing boats, gulls, the same water the Gospels keep returning to. Then Jerusalem: narrow stone streets, a shopkeeper calling out, a bell, a call to prayer. She has read these names her whole life. Nazareth. Capernaum. Gethsemane. Now they're under her feet, with weather, traffic and neighbors. Some pilgrims say they read the Gospels differently afterward.
screen: `A SILVER STAR IN BETHLEHEM.` → `DAWN ON THE SEA OF GALILEE.` → `PLACE NAMES UNDER HER FEET.`

segments.voice: For Christians, what makes this land holy goes back to John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Flesh means a body, and a body stands somewhere. Jesus was born in one town, grew up in another, fished and taught by a particular lake, and died outside a particular city wall. Some people call the land itself the fifth gospel. The four are written down; the fifth, they say, is the ground: the hills, the distances, the water. Walking from the lake up into the hills, a pilgrim can feel how far Jesus walked, and why his stories are full of fishermen, sheep and seeds. Next, the shrines. Churches stand over the places tradition links to the Gospel story: the grotto of the Nativity in Bethlehem, the Annunciation in Nazareth, and in Jerusalem the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, over the place of the crucifixion and the tomb. Franciscan friars care for many of these shrines on behalf of Catholics. Then, the people. The Holy Land is not a museum. Christian families live there, some in towns their families have called home for generations. Jews and Muslims hold places in the same land holy too, and live and pray there. Catholic pilgrims are encouraged to pray for everyone who lives there, and for peace. Last, the living stones. Pilgrims sometimes say the shrines are the old stones, and the local Christians are the living ones. Both are part of the visit.
screen: `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.` · `THE GROUND AS A FIFTH GOSPEL.` · `CHURCHES OVER THE STORY'S PLACES.` · `NOT A MUSEUM: PEOPLE LIVE THERE.` · then, large: `AND DWELT AMONG US.`

segments.voice: Picture one street in Jerusalem or Bethlehem in the morning: a Christian grandmother opening her shutters, a Jewish father walking his children to school, a Muslim shopkeeper sweeping his step, children everywhere. Don't sort them; hold them all together, their safety, their work, their sleep tonight. If you pray, say Lord, have mercy, once for each; if you don't, wish them peace, one by one.
The Holy Land. The places where Jesus was born, lived, died and rose, visited by pilgrims as a kind of fifth gospel, and home to people of more than one faith. Today's word.
Your line: the fifth gospel. The ground the Gospels walked on still has neighbors. See you tomorrow.
